title: Proxy + Connector Integration Discovery - Lambdalake
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
Gateway / proxy vs sidecar connector patterns
Rate limits, quotas and token-level billing implications
Observability hooks, traces, and token cost breakdowns
summary: Initial integration discovery to understand LambdaLake's architecture and constraints. Main focus on deciding between Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private, how Redwood SDKs and LangChain/LlamaIndex fit into their stack, gateway vs sidecar approach, and observability/rate limit requirements. Agreed next step: Redwood to share an architecture note, pricing, and a pilot plan; customer to provide sample traffic profile and security contacts.
transcript:
[00:00] Daniel (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro, I'm Daniel Park from Redwood, with Lina our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Markus (CTO): Good thanks. We've been wanting to talk about the integration options. We've got a couple constraints — we run a Kubernetes-heavy infra, lots of latency-sensitive customer features, and strict data residency requirements in EMEA.
[00:22] Lina (SE): Great, we'll try to map the options — hosted, dedicated, private — to those requirements and then walk through SDKs and gateway patterns.
[00:30] Priya (Platform Eng): One thing up front, we already use a gateway proxy for our internal ML infra, so we were curious whether to put Redwood behind that or use a sidecar approach per service.
[00:40] Daniel: Perfect. Before we dig deep, can you outline the main workloads you plan to run? batching? streaming? embeddings?
[00:48] Samir (PM): Mostly chat-like generation in our customer support product, some embeddings for search and reranking, and a small eval workload. Latency SLOs are around 300ms p50, 700ms p95.
[00:59] Lina: Ok and what's your expected throughput? tokens per second or requests per minute?
[01:04] Priya: For the pilot, maybe 150 RPS peak, but production could be 1k RPS across multiple services. Token lengths average 80-150 for responses.
[01:14] Daniel: That helps a lot. So we should talk about batching and KV / prefix cache — Redwood runtime can batch across requests while keeping latency SLOs if you configure concurrency and max batch windows. We also provide automatic prefix caching for repeated prompts which helps cost.
[01:30] Markus: Quick security question — do you support VPC peering and customer-managed KMS for Private deployments? We have compliance that requires keys to be under our control.
[01:38] Lina: Yes, Private has customer KMS/HSM integrations and a VPC-only control plane option. Dedicated can also be isolated by account with VPC egress controls but still hosted by Redwood; we can map that out.
[01:49] Priya: For Dedicated, is there an option to run the inference nodes in our cloud account or is it always Redwood-managed?
[01:55] Daniel: Dedicated is Redwood-managed but you get reserved capacity and network controls. For fully on-prem or air-gapped, that's under Private where the control plane is customer-managed.
[02:04] Samir: Let's talk integration patterns. Our current gateway does auth, routing, and rate limiting. Do people use Redwood behind a central gateway or adopt a per-service sidecar?
[02:15] Lina: Both are common. Central gateway -> Redwood hosted endpoints is simplest; you keep your single control plane for routing. Sidecar per service gives you lower east-west latency and finer token-level controls, but you manage the sidecars. There's also a hybrid — a local proxy that forwards to Redwood and applies local caching and quotas.
[02:33] Markus: We were also evaluating running a local lightweight forwarder to do batching and only hit Redwood when the batch fills. Is that supported?
[02:40] Lina: Yes, you can run our SDK in a local agent mode to do client-side batching. The SDK has a batcher primitive and a local KV cache plugin. It integrates with LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors — we have example repos. Note: client-side batching pushes more compute to your infra but can reduce token cost.
[02:58] Priya: About LangChain / LlamaIndex — we use both. How opinionated is Redwood's SDK? Will it fit into our existing chains and indexes?
[03:06] Daniel: Our SDK exposes a standard HTTP/REST and also first-class Python SDKs. We maintain an official LangChain wrapper and LlamaIndex connectors. Most customers drop in the wrapper and replace the base LLM client with Redwood's class. There are small differences in stream semantics sometimes, e.g., chunked events are labeled differently, so you may need a tiny shim in the event parser.
[03:28] Samir: Are there rate limit headers and per-token cost headers we can surface to our telemetry so we can break down cost per route?
[03:36] Lina: Yes — responses include token usage metadata and cost estimates, and our observability hooks can emit traces with token counts. Console dashboards also show token-level breakdowns per API key or per route.
[03:47] Markus: About quotas — we need per-team quotas and spike protection. Can Redwood do rate-limiting at the API key level plus per-route caps?
[03:56] Daniel: We support API-key level quotas and rate limits, and you can enforce per-route configs. For Dedicated/Private, you can push deeper rules for on-prem enforcement. There's also automatic graceful fallback policies — if your primary model is overloaded we can route to a cheaper variant.
[04:11] Priya: Observability — we need distributed traces correlated with our request IDs. Does Redwood accept custom trace IDs and propagate them?
[04:18] Lina: Yes, you can pass a request-id header and it will be included in logs/traces. We also support OTEL ingestion for spans; you can export to your Datadog or Lightstep.
[04:29] Samir: Cost question — how does batching interact with per-token billing? If we batch, are we billed per-token across the batch?
[04:37] Daniel: Billing is per token generated/consumed. Batching can reduce compute by better GPU utilization and reduce per-call overhead, but token billing is still token-based. However, caching and prefix reuse can significantly lower token counts.
[04:49] Markus: Any concerns with KV cache consistency if we do sidecars? We have ephemeral services scaling up and down.
[04:55] Lina: Local KV cache in sidecars is ephemeral; for cross-instance reuse you'd want a shared cache (Redis-style) or use Redwood's server-side prefix cache in Dedicated/Private which is shared across the pool.
[05:07] Priya: Our infra team will insist on SOC2 and an audit trail. Where do those logs live and what's retention?
[05:14] Daniel: We have audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and retention is configurable. For Private you can keep logs entirely inside your environment. For hosted, we have enterprise packages that increase retention to 1 year and provide linkable audit trails.
[05:27] Samir: Great. Let's sketch a pilot. We're thinking of a 2-week pilot with a small set of endpoints, run a traffic replay against real requests to measure latency and cost. Can Redwood help with replay tooling?
[05:38] Lina: Yes, we have a replay harness that can take your request logs and replay at scaled rates, capturing latency/cost and generating a report. We'll need a sample of your RPS and typical token distribution.
[05:50] Markus: For benchmarks, we need p50/p95 numbers and an estimate of per-user cost at 1k RPS.
[05:56] Daniel: We'll provide an initial runbook. For per-user cost we'll use your token distribution plus model choice; we'll give a couple of model options and quantization profiles for Dedicated to reduce unit cost.
[06:08] Priya: Any integration gotchas with LangChain streaming? We rely on streaming partial tokens for UI responsiveness.
[06:14] Lina: Streaming is supported. Differences: LangChain's streaming callback interface expects token-at-a-time events — our SDK maps streaming events but sometimes the separators differ; full examples in our LangChain wrapper repo. Also watch out for rate-limited streams when concurrency is high; there's backpressure configuration.
[06:33] Samir: Competitors — we talked to two vendors earlier, OpenCloud AI and VectorFlow. OpenCloud had lock-in concerns, VectorFlow had better on-prem options but weaker observability.
[06:44] Daniel: Good to know — we'll emphasize our hybrid options and observability.
[06:48] Priya: One more question: can we run inference nodes in eu-central region only? Data residency is strict.
[06:54] Lina: Yes, region pinning is supported. For Hosted we can restrict model serving to eu-central; Dedicated provides regional pools and Private can be entirely in your data center.
[07:03] Markus: Ok if we wanted to try a sidecar approach first — deploy a small agent that proxies calls, does batching and local caching — what's the rollout complexity?
[07:11] Lina: Typical rollout: 1) deploy agent to a canary namespace, 2) configure routing for a small percentage of traffic, 3) run replay tests and compare telemetry, 4) iterate. We have a Helm chart and a k8s operator if you prefer.
[07:25] Samir: Permissions — does the agent need broad privileges? We won't allow it admin rights.
[07:30] Lina: No, the agent only needs network egress to Redwood endpoints (or your Dedicated IPs) and permission to access local cache (optional). The operator mode needs cluster-level permissions but you can run the simpler Helm installation without cluster roles.
[07:42] Daniel: Alright maybe we should capture next steps and action items.
[07:46] Markus: Yeah.
[07:47] Daniel: Lina — can you share an architecture note that compares gateway vs sidecar for their profile and includes our replay harness instructions?
[07:53] Lina: Yep. I'll include links to the LangChain wrapper, LlamaIndex connector, and the Helm chart.
[07:58] Daniel: I'll send pricing for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with sample unit economics for their token distribution. Also we'll include security docs — SOC2, KMS, and audit logs.
[08:08] Priya: We'll share a 48-hour sample of request logs and token distributions and introduce you to our security contact, Helena.
[08:15] Samir: Let's tentatively schedule a pilot kickoff next Monday if we can get those things exchanged.
[08:21] Daniel: Sounds good. Anything else?
[08:24] Markus: No, thanks.
[08:26] Daniel: Great, we'll follow up with the docs and a proposed pilot plan. Thanks everyone.
[08:31] (call ends)
